Engineering Tunable Kagome Moiré Superlattices in Twisted Transition Metal Dichalcogenides

Adrian Fedorko Affiliation: Department of Physics, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, Pennsylvania 16802, USA    Chao-Xing Liu Affiliation: Department of Physics, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, Pennsylvania 16802, USA Affiliation: Center for Theory of Emergent Quantum Matter, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, Pennsylvania 16802, USA    Zhen Bi Email: zjb5184@psu.edu Affiliation: Department of Physics, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, Pennsylvania 16802, USA Affiliation: Center for Theory of Emergent Quantum Matter, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, Pennsylvania 16802, USA
Abstract

Kagome systems are an ideal platform for exploring strongly correlated phases due to their unique electronic structure and geometric frustration. While recent solid-state realizations have uncovered a wealth of correlated states, they suffer from key limitations, including limited tunability of carrier density and interaction strength. Here, we propose an experimentally viable scheme to realize a breathing kagome moiré superlattice using a twisted trilayer of transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs). By twisting the top and bottom layers relative to the middle by small angles θ\theta and 2​θ2\theta, respectively, we generate a kagome-like moiré potential on the central layer. Continuum model calculations reveal isolated kagome bands featuring flat bands, Dirac points with tunable gaps, and van Hove singularities. Crucially, this platform offers unprecedented control over band structure, carrier density, and interactions—achievable via twist angle and electrostatic gating. Our work opens a new route to realizing clean, tunable kagome metals and provides a versatile platform for studying strongly correlated and topological phenomena.

I Introduction

The kagome lattice[74] – a two-dimensional network of corner-sharing triangles – has been a focal point in the study of strongly correlated electronic states and exotic quantum phases of matter. Its unique geometry gives rise to a wealth of unconventional behaviors, including flat electronic bands, Dirac cones, and inherent geometric frustration. These characteristics make the kagome lattice an ideal platform to explore emergent states such as quantum spin liquids[68, 89, 3, 5], topologically nontrivial phases[16, 75, 87], and unconventional superconductivity[32, 34, 79].

Cu-based compounds such as herbertsmithite, kapellasite, and haydeeite have been extensively studied for their potential quantum spin liquid behavior[53, 73, 20, 45, 26, 18, 22, 55]. More recently, the AV3Sb5 family (with A = Cs, Rb, K) has attracted attention for the coexistence of superconductivity and charge-density wave order[56, 58, 57, 91, 30, 38, 94, 11], while iron-based kagome compounds like FeSn and Fe3Sn2 are notable for their flat bands and Dirac fermion states[90, 31, 37]. Magnetic kagome systems, including Co3Sn2S2, Mn3Sn, and Mn3Ge, have also been recognized for exhibiting large anomalous Hall effects and topological semimetallic behavior[36, 50, 51, 21]. However, these materials often face challenges such as structural distortions, chemical disorder, and – more importantly – a limited tunability of their electronic structure, charge density, and interaction strength. These motivate the search for new kagome systems with enhanced material quality and controllability.

Moiré materials[1, 47] – including twisted graphene systems[4] and transition metal dichalcogenides[81, 82] (TMDs) – offer exceptional tunability in electronic structure and many-body correlations. Their success has revealed a wealth of strongly correlated phenomena, ranging from correlated insulating states[7, 9, 76, 66, 78, 39, 88] and unconventional superconductivity[8, 10, 41, 60, 54, 17, 85, 19] to integer and fractional anomalous quantum Hall effects[72, 40, 6, 59, 92, 42, 14]. External knobs such as electrostatic gating, magnetic fields, pressure, and twist angle enable control of these systems, providing a versatile platform for engineering novel quantum phases. In this work, we demonstrate that twisted homotrilayer TMDs can be harnessed to realize kagome moiré lattices, potentially opening new avenues for investigating strongly correlated electrons on kagome lattices.

II Kagome Moiré superlattices

II.1 Twist scheme and moiré potential

The twist scheme we designed stems from the observation that a kagome lattice can be formed by removing one quarter of the sites from a triangular lattice, where the removed sites lie on a larger triangular lattice with twice the original lattice constant, as shown in Fig. 1(a). In practice, the initial triangular lattice is given by moiré potentials from twisted bilayers of TMD materials, while the larger triangular lattice for site removal can be achieved by twisting another TMD layer with half of the twist angle, and hence, twice the moiré lattice constant. The twist scheme is shown in Fig. 1(b). We will show that overlaying these two moiré potentials is possible to generate a breathing kagome lattice potential on the middle layer.

We begin by analyzing the moiré potentials within the continuum model for AA-stacked twisted TMD homobilayers11 1 AA-stacking refers to the arrangement in which one monolayer is placed directly atop another, maintaining identical orientation and atomic positions in the plane. On the other hand, AB-stacking refers to the cases where the two layers are rotated by 180 degrees.. Let us consider layer A (top) is twisted counterclockwise relative to layer B (bottom) by an angle θ\theta. In the simplest version of the continuum model for twisted TMDs – where only the first harmonic potential is considered – the moiré potential on each layer is modeled by the following form[82]:

V∓A​B​(𝒓)=2​V​∑j=13cos⁡(𝒈jA​B⋅𝒓∓ψ)V_{\mp}^{AB}(\bm{r})=2V\sum_{j=1}^{3}\cos{\left(\bm{g}^{AB}_{j}\cdot\bm{r}\mp\psi\right)} (1)

where 𝒈jA​B\bm{g}_{j}^{AB}’s are the reciprocal lattice vectors of the moiré lattice formed by layers A and B, and the VV and ψ\psi are material specific parameters. Here the −/+-/+ in V∓A​B​(𝒓)V_{\mp}^{AB}(\bm{r}) labels the potential on the top (A)/bottom (B) layer. The maxima of this potential form a triangular lattice for generic values of VV and ψ\psi22 2 Except at special values of ψ\psi such as ψ=60∘\psi=60^{\circ} with V>0V>0, where the potential forms a honeycomb lattice.. The position and shape of the maxima of the potential depend on the parameter ψ\psi.

Overlapping two moiré potentials to form a kagome potential can be done with three twisted TMD layers, since the middle layer will feel the moiré potentials from both sides. More explicitly, the potential that layer B experiences will be a combination of the AB and the BC moiré potentials. If the lattice constant of one moiré potential is twice that of the other, the resulting maxima experienced by layer B can arrange into a kagome lattice. In this work, we consider the case where all three layers are composed of the same TMD material. We briefly comment on other cases in the discussion.

To form a kagome potential, the layers must be twisted so that the lattice constant for the AB moiré lattice is twice that of the BC moiré lattice (i.e., |aMA​B/aMB​C|=2\left|a_{M}^{AB}/a_{M}^{BC}\right|=2). Equivalently, the relative twist angles must satisfy |θB​C/θA​B|=2|\theta_{BC}/\theta_{AB}|=2, where θl​l′=θl−θl′\theta_{ll^{\prime}}=\theta_{l}-\theta_{l^{\prime}}. In principle, one can implement either a helical twist (θB​C=2​θA​B\theta_{BC}=2\theta_{AB}) or an alternating twist (θB​C=−2​θA​B\theta_{BC}=-2\theta_{AB}). In this work, we adopt the alternating-twist configuration by choosing θA=θ\theta_{A}=\theta, θB=0\theta_{B}=0, and θC=2​θ\theta_{C}=2\theta, which yields θA​B=θ\theta_{AB}=\theta and θB​C=−2​θ\theta_{BC}=-2\theta (see Appendix A).

In the alternating twist case, the combined moiré potential felt by the middle layer can be written as

V+A​B​(𝒓)+V−B​C​(𝒓)\displaystyle V^{AB}_{+}(\bm{r})+V^{BC}_{-}(\bm{r})
=2​V​∑j=13(cos⁡(𝒈jA​B⋅𝒓+ψ)+cos⁡(𝒈jB​C⋅𝒓−ψ))\displaystyle=2V\sum_{j=1}^{3}\left(\cos{\left(\bm{g}_{j}^{AB}\cdot\bm{r}+\psi\right)}+\cos{\left(\bm{g}_{j}^{BC}\cdot\bm{r}-\psi\right)}\right)
=2​V​∑j=13(cos⁡(𝒈jA​B⋅𝒓+ψ)+cos⁡(2​𝒈jA​B⋅𝒓+ψ))\displaystyle=2V\sum_{j=1}^{3}\left(\cos{\left(\bm{g}_{j}^{AB}\cdot\bm{r}+\psi\right)}+\cos{\left(2\bm{g}_{j}^{AB}\cdot\bm{r}+\psi\right)}\right) (2)

Here, from the second to the third line, we use the fact 𝒈jB​C≅−2​𝒈jA​B\bm{g}_{j}^{BC}\cong-2\bm{g}_{j}^{AB} for the alternating twist. The shape of the moiré potential depends crucially on the parameter ψ\psi. We treat ψ\psi as a tuning parameter and plot the moiré potential as a function of ψ\psi in Fig. 1(c). We find three distinct regimes based on the number of potential maxima: for 0∘<ψ<63.65∘0^{\circ}<\psi<63.65^{\circ}, the maxima form a triangular lattice. For 63.65∘<ψ<156.716∘63.65^{\circ}<\psi<156.716^{\circ}, the maxima form a breathing kagome lattice. For 156.716∘<ψ<180∘156.716^{\circ}<\psi<180^{\circ}, the maxima form a honeycomb lattice. The potentials for −ψ-\psi are identical to those for ψ\psi, except that they are rotated by 180∘180^{\circ} in real space. Strikingly, a substantial portion of the parameter space yields a kagome-like lattice; notably, the parameters for both MoTe2 and WSe2 from Ref. [82, 27, 12, 86, 63, 77, 48] fall within this regime.

The moiré potential offers a preliminary guideline for identifying the regime where kagome physics might emerge. However, the realistic band structure is influenced by more than just the moiré potential on layer B, since layers A and C also play active roles, with significant tunneling to and from layer B. Therefore, to validate the proposed scheme, it is essential to perform a detailed continuum model calculation that incorporates all of these effects, which we will discuss next.

II.2 Continuum model and band structures

Before proceeding with the calculations, one issue must be clarified. With the twist scheme described above, the orientations of the moiré superlattices generated by the AB and BC layers are slightly rotated relative to each other. This is evident in Fig. 2(a), where the edges (𝒒1A​B\bm{q}^{AB}_{1} and 𝒒1B​C\bm{q}^{BC}_{1}) of the AB and BC moiré Brillouin zones are slightly misaligned. This effect will lead to a supermoiré pattern. The lattice constant of this supermoiré pattern is on the order of aM​MA​B,B​C∼a0/θ2a^{AB,BC}_{MM}\sim a_{0}/\theta^{2}, which, for small twist angles, is much larger than those of the individual AB and BC moiré patterns. For instance, when the twist angle θA​B\theta_{AB} is approximately 1.5∘1.5^{\circ}, the moiré lattice constant is around 10 nm, while the supermoiré lattice constant is on the order of 500 nm. Given that the electron coherence lengths in current TMD materials[52, 62] are much shorter than this, the supermoiré patterns can be safely neglected at this stage. Consequently, the band structure can be determined using only the AB and BC moiré patterns, assuming they are aligned. Although the band structure would exhibit variations on the scale of the supermoiré lattice constant, we defer the study of these variations to future work. In summary, we approximate the AB and BC moiré lattices as being commensurate (with collinear 𝑲\bm{K}-points), and the AB moiré Brillouin zones will serve as the effective Brillouin zone as shown in Fig. 2(b).

The AA-stacked twisted homotrilayer TMD continuum model for valley η=±\eta=\pm is given by the Eq. (3).

Hη​(𝒓)=(−ℏ2​𝒌^22​m∗+V−A​B​(𝒓)+D/2tηA​B​(𝒓)0tAB∗η(𝒓)−ℏ2​𝒌^22​m∗+V+A​B​(𝒓)+V−B​C​(𝒓)tηB​C​(𝒓)0tBC∗η(𝒓)−ℏ2​𝒌^22​m∗+V+B​C​(𝒓)−D/2)H_{\eta}(\bm{r})=\begin{pmatrix}-\frac{\hbar^{2}\hat{\bm{k}}^{2}}{2m^{*}}+V^{AB}_{-}(\bm{r})+D/2&t^{AB}_{\eta}(\bm{r})&0\\ t^{AB*}_{\eta}(\bm{r})&-\frac{\hbar^{2}\hat{\bm{k}}^{2}}{2m^{*}}+V^{AB}_{+}(\bm{r})+V^{BC}_{-}(\bm{r})&t^{BC}_{\eta}(\bm{r})\\ 0&t^{BC*}_{\eta}(\bm{r})&-\frac{\hbar^{2}\hat{\bm{k}}^{2}}{2m^{*}}+V^{BC}_{+}(\bm{r})-D/2\end{pmatrix} (3)

The form of the moiré potentials are given by Eq. (1) and (2). The inter-layer tunneling is given by

tηl​l′(𝒓)=w∑j=13e−ηi𝒒jl​l′⋅𝒓,t^{ll^{\prime}}_{\eta}(\bm{r})=w\sum_{j=1}^{3}{e^{-\eta\,i\,\bm{q}_{j}^{ll^{\prime}}\cdot\bm{r}}}, (4)

where the tunneling strength ww is material dependent, ll and l′l^{\prime} label layers. Here, the moiré scattering momentum is 𝒒1l​l′=𝑲l−𝑲l′\bm{q}_{1}^{ll^{\prime}}=\bm{K}_{l}-\bm{K}_{l^{\prime}} and rotations of 𝒒1l​l′\bm{q}_{1}^{ll^{\prime}} give 𝒒jl​l′=𝒞3j−1​𝒒1l​l′\bm{q}_{j}^{ll^{\prime}}=\mathcal{C}_{3}^{j-1}\bm{q}_{1}^{ll^{\prime}}. The moiré reciprocal lattice vectors 𝒈jl​l′\bm{g}^{ll^{\prime}}_{j} are given by 𝒈jl​l′=𝒞3j−1​𝒈1l​l′=𝒒j+2l​l′−𝒒j+1l​l′\bm{g}^{ll^{\prime}}_{j}=\mathcal{C}_{3}^{j-1}\bm{g}^{ll^{\prime}}_{1}=\bm{q}_{j+2}^{ll^{\prime}}-\bm{q}_{j+1}^{ll^{\prime}}. DD is the vertical displacement field which is an external parameter. The degrees of freedom in the two valleys are related by time reversal symmetry.

The parameters used for MoTe2[82] are V=8V=8 meV, w=−8.5w=-8.5 meV, ψ=−89.6∘\psi=-89.6^{\circ}, a=3.472a=3.472 Å, and m∗=0.62​mem^{*}=0.62\,m_{e}, where mem_{e} is the electron mass. We plot the band structure from the continuum model for θ≡θA​B=1.2∘\theta\equiv\theta_{AB}=1.2^{\circ} in Fig. 3. The path in kk-space is shown in yellow in Fig. 2(b). With the MoTe2 parameters, we observe discernible kagome band structures up to θ∼1.5∘\theta\sim 1.5^{\circ}. We also analyze the band structure with WSe2 parameters; the results are detailed in the Appendix B.

The moiré kagome lattice realized in our construction has lower symmetry than an ideal kagome lattice. Within the commensurate continuum description, the single-valley Hamiltonian is invariant under translations of the enlarged moiré unit cell and under the threefold rotation C3​zC_{3z}. In contrast to the D6​hD_{6h} point-group symmetry of an ideal kagome lattice, the alternating-twist geometry distinguishes the right- and left-pointing triangles and generically breaks sixfold rotation, inversion, and unitary mirror symmetries. The resulting structure is therefore a breathing kagome lattice with only exact C3C_{3} point-group symmetry. In particular, the two inequivalent corners κ\kappa and κ′\kappa^{\prime} of the moiré Brillouin zone are not required to be degenerate. The complete two-valley Hamiltonian additionally preserves microscopic time-reversal symmetry 𝒯\mathcal{T}, which exchanges the two valleys and relates their Berry curvatures and Chern numbers. We emphasize that moiré translation symmetry is exact only within the commensurate approximation adopted here; in the physical trilayer it is weakly modulated on the much longer supermoiré length scale.

Nevertheless, the top three bands of this moiré system strongly resemble a kagome band structure. The layer polarization of the Bloch wavefunctions is depicted using RGB colors, with the layers A, B, and C represented by green, blue, and red, respectively. As shown in Fig. 3, these top three bands are almost entirely localized on layer B and are energetically well separated from the rest of the moiré bands without any additional tuning.

A comment on the band ordering is in order. For electrons in a conventional kagome confining potential, the kagome flat band is expected to appear at the top of the relevant three-band manifold. In our continuum Hamiltonian Eq. (3), however, the kinetic term −ℏ2𝒌^2/2m∗-\hbar^{2}\hat{\bm{k}}^{2}/2m^{*} describes holes in the TMD valence band, for which the moiré potential maxima act as confining wells. The resulting particle-hole conjugation reverses the band ordering, placing the kagome flat band at the bottom of the upper three-band manifold. Reaching the flat band therefore requires populating the two dispersive kagome bands above it, corresponding to a moderate hole doping that is well within the range routinely accessible by electrostatic gating in moiré TMD devices.

However, we emphasize that tunneling between layers A and B actually brings the system closer to the ideal kagome band structure. If the tunneling between layers B and C is turned off (tηB​C​(𝒓)=0t^{BC}_{\eta}(\bm{r})=0), the band structure still resembles kagome bands. In contrast, if the tunneling between A and B layers is turned off (tηA​B​(𝒓)=0t^{AB}_{\eta}(\bm{r})=0), the band gap at the 𝜿\bm{\kappa}-points becomes much larger, indicating a much more pronounced “breathing” effect (see Appendix B for details).

The fourth band is almost completely localized on layer A. This band can be shifted in energy by tuning the vertical displacement field DD. In particular, to isolate the kagome bands, one can apply a displacement field to push the layer A band away (see Fig. 3(a)). Alternatively, raising the layer A band to interact with the kagome bands can modulate the topology of the kagome bands, as illustrated in Fig. 3(c). This additional degree of freedom adds further complexity and tunability to the model.

The Chern numbers shown in Fig. 3 reveal a non-trivial DD-dependence. At D=−10D=-10 meV the layer-A orbital is energetically separated from the kagome manifold and the top three bands carry Chern numbers (0,−1,+1)(0,-1,+1) from top to bottom, consistent with a breathing-kagome model with complex NN hoppings whose phases generate a kagome analog of the Haldane mass. As DD is increased, the layer-A band is pushed upward and eventually hybridizes with the topmost kagome band near the γ\gamma point. This hybridization inverts the band character and redistributes Chern numbers among the bands; at D=+14D=+14 meV Fig. 3(c) the top four bands carry (1,−2,2,−1)(1,-2,2,-1). The displacement field thus acts as a clean experimental knob for driving topological transitions within the kagome manifold by exchanging Berry curvature with the layer-A ancilla orbital, a feature absent in other kagome moiré platforms including the graphene-based kagome moiré proposals of Refs. 70, 71.

II.3 Wannier functions and tight-binding models

We obtain the Wannier functions for the top four bands of MoTe2 with θ=1.2∘\theta=1.2^{\circ} using Wannier90[61] and construct the corresponding tight-binding model by extracting the real-space Hamiltonian matrix elements in the Wannier basis. The first three maximally localized Wannier functions (MLWFs) are localized at the sites of the kagome lattice on layer B, as expected; the total density of one of these functions is shown in Fig. 4(a), while the other two are obtained by rotations of the MLWF about the origin by 2​π/32\pi/3 and 4​π/34\pi/3, taking it to the other two red points in Fig. 4(a). The fourth MLWF is centered at the maxima on layer A, and its total density is depicted in Fig. 4(b). The hopping parameters decay exponentially with distance. A graphical representation of the hopping parameters for the first MLWF is shown in Fig. 4(c), and one for the fourth MLWF is shown in Fig. 4(d). Restricting to nearest-neighbor hopping, symmetry divides the bonds into three classes TT, as indicated in Fig. 5. The hopping amplitude on a bond ⟨i​j⟩∈T\langle ij\rangle\in T can be parameterized as |tT|​ei​θi​j|t_{T}|e^{i\theta_{ij}}. Although the individual bond phases are gauge dependent, the accumulated phase around a closed loop is gauge invariant. We therefore define four gauge-invariant fluxes associated with the four triangular plaquettes shown in Fig. 5. In general, we find nonzero fluxes through all four plaquettes, which can be tuned smoothly with the twist angle and displacement field. Representative values are shown in Tables 2 and 3 in the Appendix. Despite the tunability, the total flux through each unit cell is 2​π2\pi. More details of the MLWFs and hopping data are provided in Appendix C.

Although the twisted trilayer lacks a microscopic mirror symmetry, its low-energy tight-binding model exhibits an approximate emergent magnetic-mirror symmetry ℳ~x=ℳx​𝒯\widetilde{\mathcal{M}}_{x}=\mathcal{M}_{x}\mathcal{T}, where ℳx\mathcal{M}_{x} denotes reflection about the xx axis as shown in Fig. 5. Although ℳx\mathcal{M}_{x} and time reversal 𝒯\mathcal{T} separately exchange the two valleys, their product preserves each valley, maps (kx,ky)(k_{x},k_{y}) to (−kx,ky)(-k_{x},k_{y}), and satisfies ℳ~x2=+1\widetilde{\mathcal{M}}_{x}^{2}=+1 for spinful Kramers valleys. Without imposing this symmetry in the Wannier construction, we find that the resulting band structure approximately satisfies En​(kx,ky)=En​(−kx,ky)E_{n}(k_{x},k_{y})=E_{n}(-k_{x},k_{y}) and that the fitted hopping amplitudes approximately obey the corresponding magnetic-mirror relations. We therefore regard ℳ~x\widetilde{\mathcal{M}}_{x} not as an exact microscopic symmetry of the twisted trilayer, but as an approximate emergent symmetry of its low-energy moiré description.

An interesting feature to note is the sublattice polarization of this kagome model. We plot the real-space distribution of the Bloch wavefunctions near the van Hove singularity (VHS), namely 𝒎\bm{m}-points, for the top three bands in Appendix D. We find that the real-space wavefunction of each 𝒎\bm{m}-point in the second band is localized on one sublattice of the kagome lattice (shown in Fig. 4(e)). The pure-sublattice character of the VHS on the middle band is particularly interesting. In the standard sublattice-interference scenario for the kagome Hubbard model, a sublattice polarized VHS suppresses the on-site bare susceptibility while enhancing nesting-driven instabilities in non-trivial angular-momentum channels. At the corresponding van Hove filling (n≅5/12n\cong 5/12 of the kagome manifold), repulsive interactions are predicted to drive instabilities toward ff-wave and chiral d±i​dd\pm id superconductivity, as well as toward bond-ordered density waves and orbital-current states [33, 83, 80]. In our platform, this filling is reached at a hole density of nh≅6×(5/12)/AMn_{h}\cong 6\times(5/12)/A_{M} per moiré unit cell, where AM=(3/2)​aM2A_{M}=(\sqrt{3}/2)a_{M}^{2} is the moiré unit cell area. For θ=1.2∘\theta=1.2^{\circ} in MoTe2, this gives aM≃16.6​nma_{M}\simeq 16.6~\mathrm{nm}, AM≃238​nm2A_{M}\simeq 238~\mathrm{nm}^{2}, and nh≃1.0×1012​cm−2n_{h}\simeq 1.0\times 10^{12}~\mathrm{cm}^{-2}, well within the range routinely accessible by electrostatic gating in moiré TMD devices.

III Tunable spin models at half-filling

While our analysis so far has focused on the noninteracting band structure, it is important to understand how electronic interactions enter in a controlled limit. We therefore consider a Hubbard interaction at half filling and analyze the large-UU regime using degenerate perturbation theory.

Starting from

H=∑iεi​ni+∑iUi​ni↑​ni↓+V,H=\sum_{i}\varepsilon_{i}n_{i}+\sum_{i}U_{i}\,n_{i\uparrow}n_{i\downarrow}+V, (5)

where VV contains the hopping processes introduced in the noninteracting model, charge fluctuations are suppressed for Ui≫|t|U_{i}\gg|t|, and the low-energy Hilbert space consists of singly occupied states. A second-order expansion in t/Ut/U yields an effective spin Hamiltonian acting within this manifold (see Appendix E).

With the approximate emergent magnetic-mirror symmetry ℳ~x\widetilde{\mathcal{M}}_{x}, the hopping amplitudes along and are related by complex conjugation. This symmetry therefore combines the two bond classes into a single class, .

This provides a controlled interacting extension of the noninteracting kagome plus hexagon center band structure discussed above. The onsite energy of the spin at the hexagon center is directly controlled by the vertical displacement field since it is localized on layer A, so the system can be continuously tuned between a pure kagome spin model (central spin pushed far above or below the kagome manifold) and a coupled kagome–triangular spin system (central spin resonant with the kagome sites). This provides a clean experimental knob to interpolate between qualitatively distinct correlated regimes within a single device.

While a complete phase-diagram analysis of Eq. (6) is beyond the scope of this work, several limiting regimes are already intriguing.

(Note that the DM interaction in our model cannot be globally gauged away by a local rotation of the spin basis, because the plaquettes carry nontrivial gauge-invariant fluxes. These fluxes can be continuously tuned by varying the twist angle and displacement field.) The ground state of the breathing-kagome Heisenberg model is the subject of active investigation: variational Monte Carlo studies have proposed both a gapped ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} spin liquid [69, 23] and a persistent gapless U(1) Dirac spin liquid [24], while DMRG and iPEPS calculations find that the isotropic spin liquid is stable to substantial breathing anisotropy, with a transition to a nematic When the layer-A orbital is tuned into resonance with the kagome manifold, the central spin couples antiferromagnetically to all six surrounding kagome sites, realizing a two-dimensional spin model in which a kagome antiferromagnet is augmented by an additional spin at every hexagon center. Closely related models have been studied previously: the spin-1/2 Heisenberg model interpolating between kagome and triangular limits via a centered spin retains 120∘ Néel order down to J′/J≃0.2J^{\prime}/J\simeq 0.2, below which antiferromagnetic correlations rapidly weaken [2]; and a classical Heisenberg model with a six-coordinated central moment coupled to surrounding kagome spins selects the 3×3\sqrt{3}\times\sqrt{3} ordering over the q=0q=0 ordering at weak to moderate coupling, with crossovers to canted and ferrimagnetic phases at stronger coupling [65]. Our platform realizes this class of models, with the central-coupling strength continuously tunable by the displacement field, providing a direct experimental testbed for these predictions.

(iii) Doping away from half filling. Light doping of the half-filled Mott insulator gives rise to a breathing-kagome tt-JJ model with complex hopping amplitudes. Previous studies of the uniform kagome tt-JJ model have proposed unconventional superconducting states [35, 29], and other competing states such as valence-bond and charge-ordered states [15, 28]. The combination of breathing anisotropy and nontrivial hopping fluxes further enriches this already subtle many-body problem, opening new opportunities for pairing and competing correlated phases beyond those of the uniform kagome model. A quantitative numerical investigation of this regime is left to future work.

A quantitative numerical analysis of these regimes is left to future work.

IV Discussion and outlook

In this work, we propose a route to achieve a kagome moiré lattice by twisting three layers of TMD materials. Our continuum model calculations exhibit a strong resemblance to the kagome band structure under this scheme. However, there are two caveats to note: 1) Our model is based on the first-harmonic continuum approximation, which is expected to perform well for intermediate twist angles. For smaller twist angles, lattice relaxation effects become significant, and it is argued that the continuum model needs to be updated to include higher-order harmonics[27, 44]. The exact models for small angles are currently under investigation, and the results have not yet converged[27, 44]. Consequently, we leave this aspect for future study. 2) As mentioned earlier, this particular twist scheme gives rise to a supermoiré lattice with a characteristic length scale of hundreds of nanometers. This implies that the continuum model band structure is valid only within regions of this size, and the band structure will vary on the scale of the supermoiré lattice. We emphasize that the validity of the local moiré band description depends on which probe is being considered. For transport experiments and any quantity dominated by the single-particle coherence length ℓcoh≪aM​M\ell_{\rm coh}\ll a_{MM}, the supermoiré variation averages out and the local band structure controls the response. For real-space probes such as STM and nano-ARPES, however, the band structure should be expected to vary continuously across the supermoiré unit cell, in analogy with the moiré mosaic observed in helical trilayer graphene [13, 84]. Understanding the impact of this mosaic physics for the kagome case is an interesting future direction.

We also note a few promising proposals for graphene-based kagome moiré systems in Refs. 70, 71 and TMD-based kagome moiré systems in Ref. 64, although they require a certain degree of parameter tuning or specific filling and interaction effects. Another related approach to realizing kagome moiré superlattices in twisted TMDs was recently proposed in Ref. 49. While this work also demonstrates the emergence of kagome moiré superlattices, the underlying mechanisms differ. Their construction relies on a lateral displacement between same-angle, helically twisted layers, whereas our construction employs alternating twist angles without any relative shift. As a result, the band structures and tunability are distinct. For example, the tunable fourth band from the top that is localized on layer A is unique to our approach. We also emphasize that our approach may offer a general route to engineering line-graph moiré superlattices. The kagome lattice is the line graph of the honeycomb lattice, and our construction realizes it from a triangular moiré potential by selectively suppressing one quarter of the maxima with a commensurate longer-wavelength potential. The same principle could generalize to other parent lattices: applying the alternating-twist scheme to a square-lattice material, for instance, may have the potential to realize a Lieb-lattice moiré, with the longer-wavelength potential suppressing the appropriate sublattice of the parent square moiré. We leave a detailed exploration of such generalizations to future work.

Now we turn to whether trilayers composed of different TMD materials can be used to realize a kagome lattice. Unfortunately, in general, this approach does not work. The desired 1:2 ratio of moiré lattice constants can always be satisfied by a combination of mismatch and twist. However, once a lattice mismatch is present, the orientation of the resulting moiré patterns becomes highly sensitive to the mismatch value and the twist angle. Even if the 1:2 lattice constant ratio is achieved, the two moiré patterns are typically misaligned by a significant angle, which does not produce a kagome lattice. Nevertheless, by exploring the extensive library of TMD materials, one may identify cases where the lattice mismatches alone can yield moiré lattice constants that are approximately in a 1:2 ratio. For instance, consider a trilayer system composed of WTe2, WSe2, and MoS2, with lattice constants 3.55Å[95], 3.28Å[95], and 3.16Å[43], respectively. Assuming perfect alignment of their crystal orientations, the moiré pattern generated by WTe2 and WSe2 has a lattice constant of 4.67nm, while that from WSe2 and MoS2 has a lattice constant of 8.96nm, resulting in a roughly 1:2 ratio. One might then expect a similar kagome band structure in this case. A survey of available TMD materials may reveal more examples where a kagome moiré lattice could be viable. Of course, a detailed study of the band structure for these cases would require an advanced continuum model or large-scale DFT calculations, which we leave for future work.

Appendix A Continuum model for twisted TMD

The AA-stacked TMD homobilayer continuum model Hamiltonian between two adjacent layers (A and B) is given by Eq. (7)[82], where A is on top of B and rotated by a small angle θA​B\theta_{AB} counterclockwise from B, and η=±\eta=\pm labels the valley.

HηA​B​(𝒓)=(−ℏ2​𝒌^22​m∗+V−A​B​(𝒓)tηA​B​(𝒓)tAB∗η(𝒓)−ℏ2​𝒌^22​m∗+V+A​B​(𝒓))H^{AB}_{\eta}(\bm{r})=\begin{pmatrix}-\frac{\hbar^{2}\hat{\bm{k}}^{2}}{2m^{*}}+V^{AB}_{-}(\bm{r})&t^{AB}_{\eta}(\bm{r})\\ t^{AB*}_{\eta}(\bm{r})&-\frac{\hbar^{2}\hat{\bm{k}}^{2}}{2m^{*}}+V^{AB}_{+}(\bm{r})\end{pmatrix} (7)

The moiré potential from layers A and B is approximated by including just the first harmonic of its Fourier expansion, see Eq. (8). The potentials on the top (A) and on the bottom (B) layer are given by V−A​B​(𝒓)V^{AB}_{-}(\bm{r}) and V+A​B​(𝒓)V^{AB}_{+}(\bm{r}) respectively.

V∓A​B​(𝒓)=2​V​∑j=13cos⁡(𝒈jA​B⋅𝒓∓ψ)V^{AB}_{\mp}(\bm{r})=2V\sum_{j=1}^{3}\cos{\left(\bm{g}_{j}^{AB}\cdot\bm{r}\mp\psi\right)} (8)

The amplitude VV and phase ψ\psi are parameters that are material specific. The moiré reciprocal lattice vectors 𝒈jA​B\bm{g}^{AB}_{j} are given by 𝒈jA​B=𝒞3j−1​𝒈1A​B=𝒒j+2A​B−𝒒j+1A​B\bm{g}^{AB}_{j}=\mathcal{C}_{3}^{j-1}\bm{g}^{AB}_{1}=\bm{q}_{j+2}^{AB}-\bm{q}_{j+1}^{AB} where 𝒒1A​B=𝑲A−𝑲B\bm{q}_{1}^{AB}=\bm{K}_{A}-\bm{K}_{B}, and 𝒒jA​B=𝒞3j−1​𝒒1A​B\bm{q}_{j}^{AB}=\mathcal{C}_{3}^{j-1}\bm{q}_{1}^{AB}. The potential respects C3C_{3} symmetry. The positions and shape of maxima of the potential depend on the parameter ψ\psi. We plot a few examples of the potentials for different values of ψ\psi in Fig. 6.

The inter-layer tunneling amplitude between layers A and B is given by Eq. (9), where the parameter ww is known as the tunneling strength.

tηA​B(𝒓)=w∑j=13e−ηi𝒒jA​B⋅𝒓t^{AB}_{\eta}(\bm{r})=w\sum_{j=1}^{3}{e^{-\eta\,i\,\bm{q}_{j}^{AB}\cdot\bm{r}}} (9)

The Hamiltonian in Ref. [82] is related to the Hamiltonian in Eq. (7) by a unitary transformation H~ηA​B​(𝒓)=Uη​(𝒓)​HηA​B​(𝒓)​Uη†​(𝒓)\widetilde{H}^{AB}_{\eta}(\bm{r})=U_{\eta}(\bm{r})H^{AB}_{\eta}(\bm{r})U^{\dagger}_{\eta}(\bm{r}) where Uη​(𝒓)U_{\eta}(\bm{r}) is given by Eq. (10). The benefit of the form in Eq. (9) is that the 𝒞3\mathcal{C}_{3} symmetry is manifest since HηA​B​(𝒞3​𝒓)=HηA​B​(𝒓)H^{AB}_{\eta}(\mathcal{C}_{3}\bm{r})=H^{AB}_{\eta}(\bm{r}).

Uη​(𝒓)=(eη​i​𝑲A⋅𝒓00eη​i​𝑲B⋅𝒓)U_{\eta}(\bm{r})=\begin{pmatrix}e^{\eta i\bm{K}_{A}\cdot\bm{r}}&0\\ 0&e^{\eta i\bm{K}_{B}\cdot\bm{r}}\end{pmatrix} (10)

For three twisted layers, the moiré potential on layer B is given by Eq. (11) since layer B is the bottom layer in the AB moiré system and the top layer in the BC moiré system.

V+A​B​(𝒓)+V−B​C​(𝒓)=2​V​∑j=13(cos⁡(𝒈jA​B⋅𝒓+ψ)+cos⁡(𝒈jB​C⋅𝒓−ψ))V^{AB}_{+}(\bm{r})+V^{BC}_{-}(\bm{r})=2V\sum_{j=1}^{3}\left(\cos{\left(\bm{g}_{j}^{AB}\cdot\bm{r}+\psi\right)}+\cos{\left(\bm{g}_{j}^{BC}\cdot\bm{r}-\psi\right)}\right) (11)

Knowing that to get a kagome lattice the ratio of the twist angles must be |θB​C/θA​B|=2|\theta_{BC}/\theta_{AB}|=2, one can choose either a helical twist or alternating twist. We can first check if θB​C=2​θA​B\theta_{BC}=2\theta_{AB} produces a kagome lattice. The moiré potential is given by

V+A​B​(𝒓)+V−B​C​(𝒓)=2​V​∑j=13(cos⁡(𝒈jA​B⋅𝒓+ψ)+cos⁡(2​𝒈jA​B⋅𝒓−ψ)),V^{AB}_{+}(\bm{r})+V^{BC}_{-}(\bm{r})=2V\sum_{j=1}^{3}\left(\cos{\left(\bm{g}_{j}^{AB}\cdot\bm{r}+\psi\right)}+\cos{\left(2\bm{g}_{j}^{AB}\cdot\bm{r}-\psi\right)}\right), (12)

using 𝒈jB​C=2​𝒈jA​B\bm{g}_{j}^{BC}=2\bm{g}_{j}^{AB}. It turns out that this scheme does not produce a kagome lattice for any value of ψ\psi. The lattice with a larger lattice constant always lowers the potential of three of the triangular sublattices, instead of just one, as shown in Fig. 7(a). Consequently, it only produces a triangular lattice for any ψ\psi.

However, with an alternating twist, the situation is reversed. If θB​C=−2​θA​B\theta_{BC}=-2\theta_{AB}, the potential on layer B is then given by Eq. (13), since 𝒈jB​C=−2​𝒈jA​B\bm{g}_{j}^{BC}=-2\bm{g}_{j}^{AB}. A plot of these two moiré potentials adding up to make a kagome potential is in Fig. 7(b). We can also see the kagome potential is breathing as the kagome triangles pointing right have a different potential shape than the triangles pointing left. This is expected as our system has a lower symmetry than the ideal kagome lattice.

V+A​B​(𝒓)+V−B​C​(𝒓)=2​V​∑j=13(cos⁡(𝒈jA​B⋅𝒓+ψ)+cos⁡(2​𝒈jA​B⋅𝒓+ψ))V^{AB}_{+}(\bm{r})+V^{BC}_{-}(\bm{r})=2V\sum_{j=1}^{3}\left(\cos{\left(\bm{g}_{j}^{AB}\cdot\bm{r}+\psi\right)}+\cos{\left(2\bm{g}_{j}^{AB}\cdot\bm{r}+\psi\right)}\right) (13)

Appendix B More band structure results

In this section, we present the band structures of our kagome systems with various parameters.

B.1 Varying twist angles

We plot the moiré band structure of MoTe2 using the parameters in Ref. [82] for various twist angles in Fig. 8. We can observe that there are discernible kagome bands up to a twist angle of θ=1.5∘\theta=1.5^{\circ}.

B.2 WSe2 at different angles

We repeat the same plots of the band structure as a function of θ\theta using the DFT parameters for WSe2 from [12].

B.3 Different continuum model parameters

Here we calculate the moiré band structure for our twisting scheme with different parameters from Ref. [82, 86, 12], shown in Fig. 10. They show qualitatively similar kagome behaviors. The parameters used are in Table 1.

B.4 Varying tunneling strength

One observation is that the tunneling between layers A and B plays an interesting role, as it pushes the band structure towards the ideal kagome band structure by closing the gap at the 𝜿\bm{\kappa}-points. The gaps open again and continue to widen as the tunneling is further increased. In this subsection, we treat the tunneling parameter as a knob and plot the band structure as function of the tunneling strength. For simplicity, we fix the twist angle θ=1.2∘\theta=1.2^{\circ} and use the MoTe2 parameters in Ref. [82].

If we completely turn off the tunneling (result in Fig. 11(a)), we find that the top three blue bands have a large gap at the Dirac point. This signifies a strong breathing lattice. This limit of zero tunneling will correspond to the physical case when we have the three layers starting from AB stacking instead of AA stacking. Because of the strong spin-orbit coupling, valley and spin degree of freedom in TMDs are locked. And if we start from the AB stacking, the tunneling between layers are suppressed due to spin mismatch[93].

As we dial up the tunneling, we see that the Dirac gaps become smaller (and they are not symmetric for 𝜿\bm{\kappa} and 𝜿′\bm{\kappa}^{\prime}). The Dirac gaps close and then reopen successively as we increase ww. In the large ww regime, again the band structure shows strong breathing (non-ideal) kagome behavior. The band structure in Fig. 11 shows that there is a region around w=−9w=-9 meV where the Dirac gaps are very small. Interestingly, when the tunneling between layers B and C is turned off, the band structure still resembles the kagome band structure, whereas if the tunneling between layers A and B is turned off, the Dirac gaps get much wider and the band structure no longer looks like that of a kagome lattice. Since the breathing kagome band structure is a result of the mismatch of the hoppings between right- and left-pointing triangles, the fact that tunneling to layer A reduces the breathing (for some range of ww) suggests that tunneling to and from layer A effectively reduces the difference between the hoppings of the right- and left-pointing triangles.

Wannier90[61] was used to find the maximally localized Wannier functions for the top four bands in Fig. 11(c). The parameters for this Hamiltonian are from Ref. [82]. First, the Hamiltonian was diagonalized, providing the energies εn​𝒌\varepsilon_{n\bm{k}} and wavefunctions |ϕn​𝒌⟩\ket{\phi_{n\bm{k}}} at each point in the chosen 𝒌\bm{k}-mesh in the first Brillouin zone. The input to Wannier90 included wavefunction overlaps, initial projections, and the eigenvalues εn​𝒌\varepsilon_{n\bm{k}} for the top four bands.

The wavefunction overlaps are given by Eq. (14), where the vector 𝒃\bm{b} is the vector between adjacent 𝒌\bm{k}-points in the 𝒌\bm{k}-mesh.

Mm​n(𝒌,𝒃)≡⟨ϕm​𝒌|e−i𝒃⋅𝒓^|ϕn​𝒌+𝒃⟩M_{mn}^{(\bm{k},\bm{b})}\equiv\braket{\phi_{m\bm{k}}|e^{-i\bm{b}\cdot\hat{\bm{r}}}|\phi_{n\bm{k}+\bm{b}}} (14)

Wannier90 also needed starting guesses for the Wannier orbitals. These were passed in as projections Am​n​(𝒌)A_{mn}(\bm{k}), see Eq. (15), of the Bloch states onto the trial localized orbitals |gn⟩\ket{g_{n}}. The trial orbitals chosen are given in Eq. (16), where 𝒓n\bm{r}_{n} is the initial guess for the nnth Wannier center, σn\sigma_{n} is a guess for the standard deviation of the nnth Wannier function, and the fl​nf_{ln} are layer weights such that ∑l|fl​n|2=1\sum_{l}|f_{ln}|^{2}=1.

Am​n​(𝒌)≡N​⟨ϕm​𝒌|gn⟩A_{mn}(\bm{k})\equiv\sqrt{N}\braket{\phi_{m\bm{k}}|g_{n}} (15)
gl​n​(𝒓)≡⟨𝒓,l|gn⟩=fl​nπ​σn​e−12​σn2​(𝒓−𝒓n)2g_{ln}(\bm{r})\equiv\braket{\bm{r},l|g_{n}}=\frac{f_{ln}}{\sqrt{\pi}\sigma_{n}}e^{-\frac{1}{2\sigma_{n}^{2}}(\bm{r}-\bm{r}_{n})^{2}} (16)

The maximally localized Wannier functions for the top four bands (wi​(𝒓)w_{i}(\bm{r}) for i=1,2,3,4i=1,2,3,4) are constructed using Wannier90, and the tight-binding model is obtained by extracting the real-space Hamiltonian matrix elements in the Wannier basis. Although the symmetry-adapted Wannier functions option in Wannier90 was not used to enforce C3C_{3} symmetry, the resulting Wannier functions and extracted tight-binding parameters exhibited approximate C3C_{3} symmetry. The magnitude squared and the phase of the Wannier orbitals are plotted in Fig. 12. We also present the tight-binding band structure, including hopping terms up to third nearest neighbors, and compare it with the continuum model in Fig. 13. The tight-binding model reproduces the essential features of the band structure reasonably well. The fluxes acquired from hopping around the symmetry-inequivalent triangular plaquettes are labeled in Fig. 5, and the flux values as a function of twist angle are given in Table 2.

Appendix D Sublattice polarization of the van Hove singularity

Plots of the norm squared of the real-space wavefunction |ϕn​𝒌​(𝒓)|2=|⟨𝒓|ϕn​𝒌⟩|2|\phi_{n\bm{k}}(\bm{r})|^{2}=|\braket{\bm{r}|\phi_{n\bm{k}}}|^{2} in Fig. 14 show that the wavefunctions for the three inequivalent 𝒎\bm{m}-points (for the top three bands) are localized on the three sublattices of the kagome lattice. The 𝒎\bm{m}-points in these bands have Van Hove singularities (VHSs). Similar to the ideal kagome lattice, the wavefunctions of the 𝒎\bm{m}-points have sublattice polarization in real space. Band 2 has a p-type (sublattice pure) VHS, while bands 1 and 3 have m-type (sublattice mixing) VHSs.

Appendix E Strong-Coupling Expansion and Effective Spin Hamiltonian

In this appendix we present the derivation of the effective spin Hamiltonian obtained in the strong-coupling limit of the Hubbard model. The analysis follows standard degenerate perturbation theory and is included for completeness.

E.1 Degenerate Perturbation Theory

We consider a Hamiltonian decomposed into a solvable part H0∼UH_{0}\sim U and a perturbation V∼tV\sim t,

H=H0+V.H=H_{0}+V.

Let PP denote the projector onto the low-energy manifold and define Q=I−PQ=I-P. Inserting I=P+QI=P+Q and using P​H0​Q​|ψ⟩=0PH_{0}Q\ket{\psi}=0, we obtain

E​P​|ψ⟩=P​H​|ψ⟩=(P​H​P+P​V​Q)​|ψ⟩.EP\ket{\psi}=PH\ket{\psi}=(PHP+PVQ)\ket{\psi}.

Projecting instead onto the complementary subspace yields

E​Q​|ψ⟩=Q​H​|ψ⟩=(Q​H0​Q+Q​V)​|ψ⟩\displaystyle EQ\ket{\psi}=QH\ket{\psi}=(QH_{0}Q+QV)\ket{\psi}
⇒\displaystyle\Rightarrow (Q⁡(H0−E)​Q)​Q​|ψ⟩=−Q​V​|ψ⟩\displaystyle(Q(H_{0}-E)Q)Q\ket{\psi}=-QV\ket{\psi}
⇒\displaystyle\Rightarrow Q​|ψ⟩=−Q​(H0−E)−1​Q​V​|ψ⟩.\displaystyle Q\ket{\psi}=-Q(H_{0}-E)^{-1}QV\ket{\psi}.

The final step follows from the fact that PP projects onto eigenspaces of H0H_{0}, implying [H0,Q]=[P,H0]=0[H_{0},Q]=[P,H_{0}]=0, and hence Q​(H0−E)−1​Q​(Q⁡(H0−E)​Q)=QQ(H_{0}-E)^{-1}Q(Q(H_{0}-E)Q)=Q. Substituting this expression for Q​|ψ⟩Q\ket{\psi} back into the projected equation for P​|ψ⟩P\ket{\psi} gives

E​P​|ψ⟩=(P​H​P−P​V​Q​(H0−E)−1​Q​V)​|ψ⟩\displaystyle EP\ket{\psi}=(PHP-PVQ(H_{0}-E)^{-1}QV)\ket{\psi}
⇒\displaystyle\Rightarrow E​P​|ψ⟩=(P​H​P−P​V​Q​(H0−E0)−1​Q​V​P)​|ψ⟩.\displaystyle EP\ket{\psi}=(PHP-PVQ(H_{0}-E_{0})^{-1}QVP)\ket{\psi}.

In the final line we retain only terms up to second order in t/Ut/U. Inserting I=P+QI=P+Q into the second term generates contributions requiring an additional substitution for Q​|ψ⟩Q\ket{\psi}, which scale as O⁡(t3/U2)O(t^{3}/U^{2}) and are neglected. Likewise, expanding E=E0+δ​EE=E_{0}+\delta E produces corrections of order δ​E​Q​|ψ⟩∼O⁡(t3/U2)\delta E\,Q\ket{\psi}\sim O(t^{3}/U^{2}), since δ​E∼O⁡(t2/U)\delta E\sim O(t^{2}/U) and Q​|ψ⟩∼O⁡(t/U)Q\ket{\psi}\sim O(t/U). These terms are also discarded. The resulting second-order effective Hamiltonian is therefore

Heff=E0​P+P​V​P−P​V​Q​(H0−E0)−1​Q​V​P.H_{\mathrm{eff}}=E_{0}P+PVP-PVQ(H_{0}-E_{0})^{-1}QVP.

H=H0+V\displaystyle H=H_{0}+V
H0=∑iεi​ni+∑iUi​ni↑​ni↓\displaystyle H_{0}=\sum_{i}\varepsilon_{i}n_{i}+\sum_{i}U_{i}\,n_{i\uparrow}n_{i\downarrow}

where σ→\vec{\sigma} denotes the Pauli matrices. The relevant identities are

ci​σ†​cj​σ​cj​σ†​ci​σ\displaystyle c^{\dagger}_{i\sigma}c_{j\sigma}c^{\dagger}_{j\sigma}c_{i\sigma} =14+σ​12​(Siz−Sjz)−Siz​Sjz,\displaystyle=\tfrac{1}{4}+\sigma\tfrac{1}{2}(S^{z}_{i}-S^{z}_{j})-S^{z}_{i}S^{z}_{j},
ci​σ†​cj​σ​cj​σ¯†​ci​σ¯\displaystyle c^{\dagger}_{i\sigma}c_{j\sigma}c^{\dagger}_{j\bar{\sigma}}c_{i\bar{\sigma}} =−Siσ​Sjσ¯,\displaystyle=-S^{\sigma}_{i}S^{\bar{\sigma}}_{j},

where σ¯\bar{\sigma} denotes the opposite spin of σ\sigma. The σ\sigma’s on the right hand side are treated as ++ or −- depending on if σ\sigma is ↑\uparrow or ↓\downarrow respectively. For example, Sj±=Sjx±i​SjyS^{\pm}_{j}=S^{x}_{j}\pm iS^{y}_{j}. Substituting these expressions and defining Ui​j≡2​((Ui+εi−εj)−1+(Uj+εj−εi)−1)−1U_{ij}\equiv 2((U_{i}+\varepsilon_{i}-\varepsilon_{j})^{-1}+(U_{j}+\varepsilon_{j}-\varepsilon_{i})^{-1})^{-1} yields

Heff=∑iεi+∑⟨i​j⟩\displaystyle H_{\mathrm{eff}}=\sum_{i}\varepsilon_{i}+\sum_{\braket{ij}} [2​(|ti​j↑|2+|ti​j↓|2)Ui​j(SizSjz−14)+4​Re​(ti​j↑​ti​j↓∗)Ui​j(SixSjx+SiySjy)\displaystyle\left[\frac{2(|t_{ij\uparrow}|^{2}+|t_{ij\downarrow}|^{2})}{U_{ij}}\left(S^{z}_{i}S^{z}_{j}-\tfrac{1}{4}\right)+\frac{4\mathrm{Re}(t_{ij\uparrow}t^{*}_{ij\downarrow})}{U_{ij}}\left(S^{x}_{i}S^{x}_{j}+S^{y}_{i}S^{y}_{j}\right)\right.
+4​Im​(ti​j↑​ti​j↓∗)Ui​j(S→i×S→j)z+12(|ti​j↑|2−|ti​j↓|2)((Ui+εi−εj)−1−(Uj+εj−εi)−1)(Siz−Sjz)].\displaystyle+\left.\frac{4\mathrm{Im}(t_{ij\uparrow}t^{*}_{ij\downarrow})}{U_{ij}}\left(\vec{S}_{i}\times\vec{S}_{j}\right)_{z}+\frac{1}{2}(|t_{ij\uparrow}|^{2}-|t_{ij\downarrow}|^{2})((U_{i}+\varepsilon_{i}-\varepsilon_{j})^{-1}-(U_{j}+\varepsilon_{j}-\varepsilon_{i})^{-1})(S^{z}_{i}-S^{z}_{j})\right].

The projectors PP are redundant and have been dropped without affecting matrix elements. This is because HeffH_{\mathrm{eff}} is constructed to act only within the low-energy manifold, and the resulting spin operators do not connect to states with double occupancy. Imposing time-reversal symmetry, ti​j↑=ti​j↓∗=|ti​j↑|​ei​θi​j↑t_{ij\uparrow}=t^{*}_{ij\downarrow}=|t_{ij\uparrow}|e^{i\theta_{ij\uparrow}}, this reduces to

Heff=∑iεi+∑⟨i​j⟩4​|ti​j↑|2Ui​j​[Siz​Sjz−14+cos⁡(2​θi​j↑)​(Six​Sjx+Siy​Sjy)+sin⁡(2​θi​j↑)​(S→i×S→j)z].H_{\mathrm{eff}}=\sum_{i}\varepsilon_{i}+\sum_{\langle ij\rangle}\frac{4|t_{ij\uparrow}|^{2}}{U_{ij}}\left[S_{i}^{z}S_{j}^{z}-\tfrac{1}{4}+\cos(2\theta_{ij\uparrow})\left(S_{i}^{x}S_{j}^{x}+S_{i}^{y}S_{j}^{y}\right)+\sin(2\theta_{ij\uparrow})(\vec{S}_{i}\times\vec{S}_{j})_{z}\right].

When lattice symmetries enforce identical hopping amplitudes on symmetry-related bonds, the effective Hamiltonian can be written in the compact form

Heff=∑iεi+∑T4​|tT|2UT​∑⟨i​j⟩∈T[Siz​Sjz−14+cos⁡(2​θi​j)​(Six​Sjx+Siy​Sjy)+sin⁡(2​θi​j)​(S→i×S→j)z],H_{\mathrm{eff}}=\sum_{i}\varepsilon_{i}+\sum_{T}\frac{4|t_{T}|^{2}}{U_{T}}\sum_{\langle ij\rangle\in T}\left[S_{i}^{z}S_{j}^{z}-\tfrac{1}{4}+\cos(2\theta_{ij})\left(S_{i}^{x}S_{j}^{x}+S_{i}^{y}S_{j}^{y}\right)+\sin(2\theta_{ij})(\vec{S}_{i}\times\vec{S}_{j})_{z}\right], (17)

where TT labels the symmetry-inequivalent bond classes of the lattice. The hopping amplitudes ti​j↑t_{ij\uparrow} are written as |tT|​ei​θi​j|t_{T}|e^{i\theta_{ij}} for bonds ⟨i​j⟩∈T\langle ij\rangle\in T. Symmetry requires all bonds in the class TT to have the same magnitude |tT||t_{T}|, although their phases θi​j\theta_{ij} may differ. The effective interaction strengths UTU_{T} are determined by the onsite energies and Hubbard interactions of the two sites connected by each bond.
